transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-03-20
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Elena Rodriguez (Aurelia CTO), Marcus Lee (Platform Engineer), Sofia Chen (Security Architect), Rahul Mehta (Infra), Tom Nguyen (Dev)

Summary (auto): Deep dive on Private VPC deployment and inference runtime impact. Discussed PrivateLink, NAT egress, subnet sizing, ENI limits, Private DNS, and runtime topics: KV cache locality, batching, quantization, and bench plan.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, today Priya and I will run through our recommended Private VPC topology and then dig into some runtime perf items — KV cache, batching, quant. If you can just say hi and role, real quick?
[00:12] Elena (Aurelia CTO): Hi this is Elena, CTO. We're mainly looking at private deployment options for production inference, especially for PII workloads.
[00:18] Marcus (Platform Eng): Marcus, platform. I'll share our subnet layout after. We have multi-AZ and NAT gateways already.
[00:22] Sofia (Security): Sofia, security. We'll focus on KMS, audit logs, and data residency.
[00:27] Priya (Redwood SE): Awesome. Quick agenda: 1) network topology - PrivateLink vs TGW/peering, 2) DNS and egress patterns (NAT), 3) runtime perf considerations - KV cache locality, batching, quantization, 4) bench plan.
[00:38] Jordan: Cool. To start, the simplest pattern we recommend for Private deployment with minimal customer changes is PrivateLink (interface endpoints) from your VPC to Redwood's VPC endpoint service. That gives private connectivity without exposing public IPs.
[00:50] Rahul (Infra): Quick question: does PrivateLink support cross-account? We are a separate account per environment.
[00:55] Priya: Yeah PrivateLink supports cross-account; you create a VPC endpoint pointing to our service in your account. Note that interface endpoints create ENIs in your subnets and will count toward ENI and IP address limits.
[01:06] Marcus: How many ENIs do you typically need? We're worried about hitting per-AZ ENI limits on smaller instance types.
[01:12] Priya: Good call. Each interface endpoint uses an ENI per AZ. For scale, the endpoints themselves don't scale per request, but if you need higher throughput you can provision multiple endpoints across AZs and use route tables/load balancer across them. Practically, for a typical deployment we'll ask for 3 subnets (one per AZ) with /24s so you have enough IPs for ENIs, pods, and the infra.
[01:33] Tom (Dev): And what about Transit Gateway? Could we do TGW instead?
[01:36] Jordan: TGW is fine if you already have a TGW and want full routing control across multiple VPCs — the tradeoff is more operational overhead and potentially more surface area to manage. PrivateLink reduces blast radius and is usually simpler for a single service integration.
[01:49] Sofia: How does this affect egress? We must log all outbound traffic through our NATs for compliance.
[01:55] Priya: With PrivateLink, traffic to Redwood stays inside AWS and doesn't egress to the internet; it flows through the ENI to our endpoint service. For other outbound calls (e.g., metrics, updates) you'd still egress via your NATs; we usually recommend routing logs and any optional callbacks through your existing NATs so you can control logging.
[02:12] Elena: What about DNS? We need split-horizon or private hosted zones.
[02:16] Priya: Yes — you'll create a private hosted zone and configure the endpoint's private DNS name, or use the interface endpoint's DNS entries. If you do custom domain names you can create CNAMEs pointing to the endpoint. Watch out for conditional forwarders if you have on-prem DNS via Direct Connect.
[02:30] Marcus: Is there any issue with ECS/EKS service discovery and kube-dns?
[02:34] Priya: Generally okay. Just ensure the VPC resolver is configured so pods can resolve the endpoint. There are occasional corner cases where cluster DNS caching collides with endpoint DNS TTLs — best to test TTL and validate clients refresh as expected.
[02:47] Jordan: Switching to runtime: a key latency factor is KV cache locality. If inference runtime Kv cache is remote across a network hop it adds tens of milliseconds for cache misses. Our recommendation is colocating KV cache on the same host or same VPC — in Private VPC deployments that means deploying Redwood runtime inside your VPC or ensuring PrivateLink paths have minimal hops.
[03:07] Marcus: So if we run Redwood Private inside our VPC, we get local KV cache?
[03:11] Priya: Exactly. If we run a private control plane and runtime inside your VPC or VPC-peered cluster, KV cache and batching have lower network latency. If the runtime is across regions or via a peered VPC with multiple hops you'll see p50/p95 tail increases.
[03:26] Elena: How big is the impact? ballpark numbers?
[03:29] Priya: For a typical LLM request 512 tokens, a remote KV cache hit might add ~10-25ms per token fetch depending on path; warm cache reduces that dramatically. Batch vs single: batching increases throughput but adds queue latency depending on your batching window — a 20ms batching window might increase median latency by 10-20ms but improves tokens/s.
[03:47] Tom: On quantization we assume INT8 gives speedups, but what about quality regression?
[03:52] Priya: Right. INT8 or 4-bit quantization is model-dependent. For many open models FP16->INT8 yields 1.5-3x throughput improvements with small quality deltas; we recommend running evals on your prompts. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles per model and workload that balance quality and throughput.
[04:10] Marcus: Are there kernel-level implications for Private VPC? I mean network doesn't change kernels, but does colocation change GPU kernel selection?
[04:16] Priya: Kernel selection is mostly about GPU type and sequence length. Where colocation helps is reducing time spent on network and serializing KV cache; that makes kernel efficiency more impactful because CPU/network overheads are lower. So yes, colocated runtimes show better effective throughput on the same kernels.
[04:31] Jordan: We also touched instrumentation: you'll want token-level latency tracing, per-route p50/p95/p99, and KV cache hit rates. Priya will provide a sample Grafana dashboard showing these metrics.
[04:42] Priya: We'll include a dashboard template. Also note batching behavior — continuous batching vs fixed-window batching — continuous typically has better latency at scale but you need predictable traffic patterns.
[04:53] Elena: For our compliance, all key material must be customer-managed (KMS/HSM). Can Redwood integrate with our KMS?
[04:59] Jordan: Yes. For Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM via standard APIs and support BYOK. We'll note the required IAM roles and the network routes for KMS endpoints in the security pack.
[05:10] Sofia: What about audit logs and retention? We need 2 years for certain flows.
[05:14] Priya: We can push audit logs into your CloudWatch/S3 buckets or to your SIEM. Retention can be configured — we'll map that in the SOW.
[05:21] Marcus: Back to NAT gateways: if we keep egress through NATs, does that affect latency for callbacks like model telemetry?
[05:27] Priya: It can. If telemetry is batched and asynchronous it's not a problem. For any synchronous callbacks you'd want them over PrivateLink as well, or ensure NAT egress is sized for low-latency with minimal SNAT collision.
[05:40] Rahul: Any IP exhaustion concerns with ENIs?
[05:43] Priya: Yes, especially in clusters with many pods. Use /24s per AZ or increase ENI limits with AWS if needed. We'll ask for current ENI quotas as part of the prep.
[05:53] Tom: For on-prem options, do you support direct-connect plus PrivateLink?
[05:57] Jordan: You can combine Direct Connect with PrivateLink — PrivateLink works over AWS's internal fabric. For on-prem-to-service you'll typically use Direct Connect to the VPC hosting the endpoints or set up a VPN plus DNS forwarding. We'll share a topology doc.
[06:09] Priya: Now performance bench plan: we propose a 3-phase test: 1) baseline single-instance latency/throughput with representative prompts and quant profiles, 2) scale-out tests with batching and concurrent clients to measure tokens/s and p99 tail, 3) network topology variations — PrivateLink vs peering and effect on KV cache hits.
[06:27] Jordan: We'll run synthetic clients from your app subnet to simulate traffic and also run real prompt evals with your prompt set to measure quality differences post-quantization.
[06:36] Elena: How long does a bench typically take?
[06:38] Priya: End-to-end bench + analysis is usually 1-2 weeks depending on scheduling. The actual runs per topology can be done in a day each.
[06:46] Marcus: What's the data flow for inference? We'll need a clear diagram.
[06:49] Priya: We'll provide a network diagram template showing subnets, endpoint ENIs, route tables, security groups, and where KV cache nodes and runtime lie.
[06:57] Sofia: On security, any required SG rules?
[07:00] Priya: Minimal: allow HTTPS (or mTLS) between your app subnets and the endpoint ENIs, restrict source CIDRs, and block public ingress. For KMS you need endpoints to KMS or allow egress to KMS private endpoints. We recommend mTLS for service auth as an additional layer.
[07:15] Tom: mTLS, ok. How do credentials work?
[07:18] Jordan: For Private deployments we support short-lived tokens and can integrate with your IdP for service accounts. We'll document the token rotation flow.
[07:25] Rahul: Any gotchas with split-horizon DNS and pod DNS caches?
[07:28] Priya: TTL and caching can cause stale resolution; set a reasonable TTL and validate kube-dns config. Also test DNS failover across AZs.
[07:37] Jordan: We should call out ENI IP usage again: if you run many endpoints or have many microservices, plan subnets accordingly.
[07:43] Elena: For encryption in transit, is TLS enough or do you recommend IPSec?
[07:46] Priya: TLS with mTLS for auth is typically sufficient; IPSec is heavier operationally. For regulated customers with extremely high security needs we can support additional tunnels.
[07:56] Marcus: Regarding routing: if we want green/blue deploys, can we have two endpoint services and shift traffic?
[08:01] Priya: Yes you can provision multiple endpoint connections and do DNS or LB-level routing. We also support canary rollouts at the application layer via our rollout features.
[08:12] Jordan: Anything else on network?
[08:13] Elena: No, that covers most. Let's move to some quick perf numbers and examples.
[08:17] Priya: Example: model X at FP16 on A100 gets ~120 tokens/s per GPU at typical seq lengths; INT8 can move that to ~250 tokens/s depending on kernel and quant quality. But network overhead can reduce effective tokens/s by 10-40% if KV cache is remote. So the delta is non-trivial.
[08:36] Tom: How do you instrument KV cache hit rate?
[08:39] Priya: We emit hit/miss metrics per model/route. Our dashboard shows KV hits as a percentage and you can correlate with latency. A warm prefix cache will show high hit rates and low token latency.
[08:48] Marcus: For batching, what's Redwood's default?
[08:51] Priya: We default to adaptive continuous batching with a small max window. You can tune the max window and prefer latency-first or throughput-first modes. We'll include recommended settings for low-latency vs high-throughput.
[09:02] Sofia: Are there any compliance constraints around telemetry leaving our VPC?
[09:05] Jordan: Telemetry can be pushed to your destinations; we don't need to pull it. We'll send a config where telemetry endpoints are your CloudWatch/Splunk/Datadog collectors inside your VPC.
[09:15] Elena: Ok last part — demo and artifacts.
[09:18] Priya: We'll attach three artifacts after the call: 1) Security pack (SOC2, ISO, KMS integration guide), 2) Network diagram template and endpoint checklist, 3) Perf plan + synthetic harness repo link and example dashboards. Links: (security pack) https://redwood.example.com/presales/aurelia-sec-pack, (diagram) https://redwood.example.com/presales/network-template, (bench) https://redwood.example.com/bench/harness-aurelia.
[09:42] Marcus: Great. We'll share our subnet CIDRs and ENI quotas in the next couple days.
[09:47] Jordan: Perfect. We'll also schedule the perf kick-off once we have CIDRs.
[09:52] Elena: Thanks, this was useful. Quick recap?
[09:55] Jordan: Recap: PrivateLink recommended for simplicity; ensure /24 per AZ to avoid ENI/IP exhaustion; use private hosted zones and validate DNS TTLs; colocate runtime or ensure minimal hops for KV cache; run quant evals; Redwood will share security pack, perf plan, and diagram; next steps and owners captured in the action items.
[10:12] Tom: Thanks all.
[10:13] Sofia: Thanks.
[10:15] (meeting ends)

Notes: The transcript contains some auto-generated timestamps and occasional transcription artifacts (e.g., "K-V cache" spelled, small pauses). Refer to attached links for presales docs and bench harness.
